about.title: Hillsborough Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Hillsborough is a quiet, low-density community of roughly 11,451 people in San Mateo County, known for large private lots, long driveways, wooded paths, and gated estates rather than busy commercial strips. That layout means many premises liability cases here involve private walkways, stairs, pool areas, or landscaping hazards on residential or estate property, rather than slip-and-falls at big-box stores. Because so much of Hillsborough is private property, these cases often hinge on whether a homeowner, property manager, or contractor knew about a hazard and had a reasonable chance to fix it before someone got hurt. Under California law, you generally need to show the property owner or occupier knew, or should have known, about the dangerous condition. Photos of the hazard, witness names, and any available surveillance or doorbell camera footage can matter a great deal. If you were hurt on someone else's property in Hillsborough, a free, no-obligation conversation with an independent attorney can help you understand what evidence to preserve and what your options are.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Hillsborough Premises Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Had Notice
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner or manager knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix or warn about it. On private estates, this can mean maintenance logs, prior complaints, or how long a hazard like a cracked walkway had existed.

items.title: Preserving Video and Physical Evidence
items.desc: Surveillance footage, doorbell cameras, and even the physical hazard itself can be removed, repaired, or overwritten within days. Acting quickly to document conditions and request footage preservation can be critical to a Hillsborough claim.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California follows pure comparative fault, meaning your recovery can be reduced by your own percentage of responsibility but isn't automatically barred if you were partly at fault. An attorney can help address how any fault-sharing argument affects your specific situation.

items.question: How long do I have to file a premises liability claim in Hillsborough?
items.answer: In most cases, California gives you two years from the date of the fall to file a lawsuit. If your fall happened on property owned by a government or public entity, the deadline is much shorter and involves an earlier claim-filing step. It's worth getting an evaluation early so you don't lose evidence or miss a deadline.

items.question: My fall happened on a private driveway or estate in Hillsborough — does that change anything?
items.answer: Many properties in Hillsborough are large private residences rather than commercial buildings, so the case often turns on whether the homeowner or a contractor maintaining the grounds knew about the hazard. Evidence like landscaping records, prior repair requests, or witness statements from staff can become especially important. An independent attorney can help figure out who is responsible before evidence disappears.

items.question: What if I was partly at fault for my own fall?
items.answer: California's comparative fault rule means you can still pursue a claim even if you share some responsibility, though your recovery may be reduced by your share of fault. This is fact-specific and often disputed, so documentation of the hazard helps support your side. Speaking with an attorney can clarify how this might apply to your situation.
